passages.happening:
“On the first day of the first month you are to set up the tabernacle, the Tent of Meeting” (verse 2). The ark goes in first, screened by the veil. Then the table, the lampstand and the gold altar of incense. Then the curtain at the entrance, the altar of burnt offering in front of it, the basin, and the courtyard around it all (verses 3-8).

“Take the anointing oil and anoint the tabernacle and everything in it; consecrate it along with all its furnishings, and it shall be holy” (verse 9). Aaron and his sons are to be washed, clothed and anointed, “so that they may also serve Me as priests” (verses 12-15).

“Moses did everything just as the LORD had commanded him” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Every part has been made. Now God tells Moses how to put it together, and when.

The day is the first day of the first month: New Year's Day. The flood story marks a new beginning on the same date, when the waters had dried from the earth. It is almost exactly a year since Israel left Egypt, and about nine months since they came to Sinai.

The order is from the inside out. The ark, with the tablets in it, goes into the inner room. The veil hides it. Then come the things of the Holy Place, then the entrance, then the altar and basin in the courtyard, and last the courtyard's wall. The notes on chapters 25 to 30 describe each piece.

Then everything is anointed. The oil set each thing apart for God's use alone. Holiness is prepared for here. It is not taken for granted.

The priests are named, but they are not yet at work. Their setting apart, commanded in these verses, is carried out in Leviticus 8.
passages.later:
Genesis says of the flood's end, “on the first day of the first month, the waters had dried up from the earth” (Genesis 8:13).

Leviticus tells how the priests were set apart: “Moses took some of the anointing oil and some of the blood that was on the altar and sprinkled them on Aaron and his garments” (Leviticus 8:30).
passages.asks: Everything was set apart for God before his glory came. Ask what in your life you have set apart for God alone. And ask whether you expect God's presence without making any room for it.

passages.happening:
“So the tabernacle was set up on the first day of the first month of the second year” (verse 17). Moses lays the bases, sets up the frames, and spreads the tent and its covering (verses 18-19).

“Moses took the Testimony and placed it in the ark” (verse 20). He brings the ark in and hangs the veil (verse 21). He sets the table on the north side and arranges the bread (verses 22-23). He sets the lampstand on the south side and lights the lamps (verses 24-25). He burns incense on the gold altar (verses 26-27). He offers the burnt offering and the grain offering on the altar outside (verse 29). He fills the basin, and he, Aaron and Aaron's sons wash (verses 30-32).

“And Moses set up the courtyard around the tabernacle and the altar, and he hung the curtain for the entrance to the courtyard. So Moses finished the work” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
Here the command becomes deed for the last time. One phrase rings through the passage: ‘just as the LORD had commanded him’. After verse 16 it comes seven times, the same number as in the making of the garments in chapter 39.

Moses does the priests' work himself on this first day. He sets out the bread, lights the lamps, burns the incense and offers the first sacrifices, because Aaron and his sons have not yet been set apart.

The tablets go into the ark. These are the second tablets, written after the calf. At the center of God's house lie the words Israel broke and God gave again, under the mercy seat.

‘So Moses finished the work.’ The words echo the creation story, where God ‘finished the work’ he had been doing. A world was finished, and God rested in it. A tent is finished, and the reader waits to see whether God will come to live in it. After chapter 33, that cannot be taken for granted.
passages.later:
Genesis says, “by the seventh day God had finished the work He had been doing” (Genesis 2:2).

When Solomon finished the temple, the same thing happened as in the next verses here: “the cloud filled the house of the LORD” (1 Kings 8:10).

Jesus prayed on the night before he died, “I have glorified You on earth by accomplishing the work You gave Me to do” (John 17:4).
passages.hard:
Exodus puts the altar of incense in front of the veil. Hebrews seems to put it inside the Most Holy Place. Which is right?

Exodus is clear. The gold altar stood in the Holy Place, in front of the veil (30:6; 40:26). Hebrews 9:3-4 lists ‘the golden altar of incense’ with the inner room and the ark.

Interpreters explain this in several ways. Some think the Greek word in Hebrews means the golden censer that the high priest carried into the inner room on the Day of Atonement; older English Bibles translate it that way. Others note that the Old Testament links the incense altar closely with the inner room. It stood directly before the ark, and Solomon's incense altar is called the altar ‘that belonged to the inner sanctuary’ (1 Kings 6:22), though it stood outside it. So the writer may mean that the altar belonged to the inner room in its use. Some scholars think he was following a tradition that placed it inside.

The writer of Hebrews says himself that he is not giving a detailed account (Hebrews 9:5). His argument, that the old sanctuary pointed to Christ's entry into heaven, does not hang on where one piece of furniture stood.
passages.asks: Moses did each thing as God had commanded, to the last curtain. Ask what God has given you to finish, and whether you are doing it his way. And ask what it would mean to end a piece of work able to say that it was done as he asked.

passages.happening:
“Then the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. Moses was unable to enter the Tent of Meeting because the cloud had settled on it, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (verses 34-35).

Whenever the cloud lifted from the tabernacle, the Israelites set out. If it did not lift, they stayed where they were until it did (verses 36-37).

“For the cloud of the LORD was over the tabernacle by day, and fire was in the cloud by night, in the sight of all the house of Israel” (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
This is where the whole book has been going. Exodus began with Israel as slaves, building store cities for Pharaoh. It ends with Israel free, having built a dwelling for God, and with God moving in.

After long lists of what Moses did, the last five verses are about what God does: the cloud covers, the glory fills. The book does not end with what Israel achieved. It ends with God's arrival.

After the calf, it was not certain that God would go with this people at all (33:3). Now his glory fills their tent in the middle of the camp. Mercy has had the last word.

‘Glory’ is kavod, the weight and shining of God's presence, the same glory that rested on Mount Sinai (24:16-17). The mountain's glory has come down to live in the camp. ‘Settled’ is shakan, to dwell, the root of mishkan, the tabernacle. The dwelling place is at last dwelt in. And ‘filled’ is the word used when God filled Bezalel with his Spirit (31:3). The God who filled the builders with skill now fills the building with himself.

When the temples of other nations were dedicated, the high point was the god's entry into his new house. Here there is no statue to carry in. The God no one can see comes in cloud and fire.

Then a surprise. Moses cannot go in. The man who spoke with God face to face is kept outside by the glory. Every command has been kept, and still there is a distance between the holy God and human beings that obedience alone does not close. That is where the next book begins. Leviticus opens with God calling to Moses from the tent, and goes on to teach how a people who sin may come near.

The cloud had led Israel since Egypt (13:21-22). In a desert, a cloud by day gives shade, and fire by night gives light and warmth. From now on the cloud decides when the people move and when they stay. God's guidance was not a map handed over once. It was a presence to be followed day by day. The book that began with a people crushed under a king ends with a people on the road, led by the God who lives among them.
passages.later:
Leviticus begins at this tent: “Then the LORD called to Moses and spoke to him from the Tent of Meeting” (Leviticus 1:1).

Numbers describes the cloud's leading: “At the LORD’s command the Israelites set out, and at the LORD’s command they camped” (Numbers 9:18).

At Solomon's temple “the priests could not stand there to minister because of the cloud; for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD” (1 Kings 8:11). Ezekiel later saw that glory leave the temple, and in a vision saw it come back: “the glory of the LORD filled the temple” (Ezekiel 43:5).

John writes, “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory” (John 1:14). At the transfiguration “a voice came from the cloud, saying, ‘This is My Son, whom I have chosen. Listen to Him!’” (Luke 9:35). Paul tells believers, “your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you” (1 Corinthians 6:19).

And the Bible's last vision completes what this chapter begins: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:3).
passages.asks: God brought his people out of Egypt so that he could live among them, and he did. Ask whether you think of God as near, in the middle of your life, or as far off. And ask whether you are willing to move when he moves and stay when he stays, even when you would choose otherwise.
